---
title: "Row & Column Verbs"
subtitle: "≈ dplyr single-table verbs: `filter()` · `arrange()` · `distinct()` · `slice_*()` · `select()` · `rename()` · `relocate()`"
jupyter: python3
---

R4DS's *Data transformation* chapter teaches dplyr's single-table verbs on
`flights`. This chapter follows the same path in Polars. The one-line
translations are in the cheatsheet; this chapter covers the defaults that
differ: where nulls go, which row survives a tie, what order rows come back
in, and which column verbs change a frame in place.

## In tidyverse {#sec-verb-tidyverse}

```r
library(dplyr)
library(nycflights13)

flights |> filter(dep_delay > 120, month == 1)
flights |> arrange(month, day, desc(dep_delay))
flights |> distinct(origin, dest, .keep_all = TRUE)
flights |> slice_max(distance, n = 3)             # 342 rows: ties are kept
flights |> slice_sample(prop = 1)                 # every row, shuffled
flights |> select(year:day, tail_num = tailnum)
flights |> relocate(starts_with("arr"), .before = dep_time)
```

dplyr makes promises about order and ties without being asked:

1. `arrange()` keeps tied rows in input order and puts `NA` last, in both
   directions.
2. `filter()` and `distinct()` keep rows in input order; `distinct()` keeps
   the first copy.
3. `slice_max()` and `slice_min()` keep ties.

Polars keeps `filter()`'s order and makes the rest opt-in. The docstrings give
the reason: preserving order "is more expensive to compute", and leaving the
choice of row open "allows more optimizations".

## Mental model {#sec-verb-model}

```text
 ROW VERBS: change the height, never touch a column     order of the result
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────      ─────────────────────────────────────────
 by predicate  filter(p)  remove(p)                     input order
 by position   head tail slice gather gather_every      input order (by definition)
 by value      sort(by)                                 tied rows: input order only with maintain_order=True
               top_k(k, by)  bottom_k(k, by)            exactly k rows; ties broken arbitrarily
 by identity   unique(subset, keep)                     arbitrary unless maintain_order=True
 by chance     sample(n | fraction, seed)               arbitrary unless shuffle=True / False

 COLUMN VERBS: change the width, never touch a row
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
 select  drop  rename  with_columns  with_row_index     return a new frame
 insert_column   df.columns = [...]                     modify the frame in place (!)
```

Read the right-hand column as the contract. Anything marked "arbitrary" can
differ between runs, and the fix is always an explicit argument
(@sec-verb-gotchas).

## Mechanics {#sec-verb-mechanics}

```{python}
#| include: false
%xmode Minimal
```

```{python}
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs
from pl_notes import datasets

flights_df = datasets.flights()    # 336,776 × 19, as nycflights13::flights
penguins_df = datasets.penguins()
```

### Filter rows {#sec-verb-filter}

Comma-separated predicates are combined with AND, as in dplyr. Equality tests
also have a keyword shorthand: each `name=value` becomes
`pl.col(name) == value`. In R, `filter(month = 1)` is the classic typo that
dplyr rejects; in Polars it is valid:

```{python}
flights_df.filter(pl.col("dep_delay") > 120, month=1, origin="JFK").select(
    "month", "day", "origin", "dest", "dep_delay"
).head(3)
```

The shorthand is only `==`. `origin=["JFK", "LGA"]` raises (use
`pl.col("origin").is_in(...)`), and `tailnum=None` compares with null, so it
keeps no rows (Polars warns).

**Nulls drop the row.** A row is kept only where the predicate is `true`;
`false` and null both drop it, as in dplyr. So `filter(p)` and `filter(~p)` do
not add up to the whole frame: rows where `p` is null are in neither.
`remove(p)` is the exact complement of `filter(p)`. It drops the rows where
`p` is `true` and keeps everything else, nulls included:

```{python}
late = pl.col("dep_delay") > 0
{
    "filter(late)": flights_df.filter(late).height,
    "filter(~late)": flights_df.filter(~late).height,
    "remove(late)": flights_df.remove(late).height,   # ~late plus the null rows
    "all rows": flights_df.height,
}
```

The 8,255 cancelled flights (null `dep_delay`) are only in `remove()`. In
dplyr the same complement is `filter(!(dep_delay > 0) | is.na(dep_delay))`.
Grouped filters such as `filter(n() > 1000, .by = dest)` are window
expressions: `pl.len().over("dest") > 1000` (see
[Window Functions](window.qmd)).

### Sort rows {#sec-verb-sort}

`sort()` takes several keys. `descending=` and `nulls_last=` each take one
bool for all keys, or a list with one bool per key; a list of the wrong length
raises a `ValueError`. This is `arrange(month, day, desc(dep_delay))` with
`NA` last:

```{python}
flights_df.sort(
    "month", "day", "dep_delay",
    descending=[False, False, True],
    nulls_last=True,
).select("month", "day", "dep_delay", "carrier", "flight").head(3)
```

Without `nulls_last=True`, nulls come first in both directions
(@sec-verb-nulls-first). Keys can also be expressions
([Expressions & Contexts](../core/expressions.qmd#sec-expr-contexts)).

**What "sorted" means for each dtype.** Numbers and dates sort by value.
Strings sort by code point: digits before letters, every uppercase letter
before every lowercase one, `"10"` before `"9"`. That matches `arrange()` in
dplyr ≥ 1.1, which uses the C locale by default (base R's `sort()` uses the
system locale). A `Categorical` sorts by its strings; an `Enum` sorts by its
level order, like a factor:

```{python}
words = pl.Series(["banana", "Apple", "apple", "Banana", "10", "9"])
{
    "String": words.sort().to_list(),
    "Categorical": words.cast(pl.Categorical).sort().to_list(),
    "Enum": words.cast(pl.Enum(["9", "10", "apple", "Apple", "banana", "Banana"])).sort().to_list(),
}
```

For a case-insensitive order, sort by an expression:
`sort(pl.col("word").str.to_lowercase())`.

### Distinct rows {#sec-verb-unique}

`unique(subset=...)` decides what a duplicate is from the `subset` columns
but always returns **every** column: it is `distinct(..., .keep_all = TRUE)`.
For `distinct(origin, dest)`, which keeps only those two, select first:
`select("origin", "dest").unique()`. `keep=` chooses which copy survives:

```{python}
sightings_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "tailnum": ["N1", "N2", "N1", "N3", "N2", "N1"],
    "seen":    [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6],
})
{
    keep: sightings_df.unique("tailnum", keep=keep, maintain_order=True).rows()
    for keep in ["first", "last", "none", "any"]
}
```

- `"first"` is `distinct(.keep_all = TRUE)`.
- `"last"` keeps the last copy, and `maintain_order=True` orders rows by where
  that copy sat: `N3` (row 4), `N2` (row 5), `N1` (row 6).
- `"none"` drops every repeated key (≈ `filter(n() == 1, .by = tailnum)`).
- `"any"`, the **default**, promises nothing about which copy survives. Here it
  picked the first ones; don't rely on that (@sec-verb-unique-defaults).

Null keys count as equal to each other, as in `distinct()`. `subset=` also
accepts expressions, so you can deduplicate on a computed key without adding it
as a column. The first penguin in each 1 kg mass band, the null band included:

```{python}
penguins_df.unique(
    subset=(pl.col("body_mass_g") / 1000).floor(), keep="first", maintain_order=True
).select("species", "island", "body_mass_g")
```

(The integer key `pl.col("body_mass_g") // 1000` would be more natural, but as
a `subset=` it panics in Polars 2.0.0, an engine bug. `// pl.lit(1000,
dtype=pl.Int64)` works.)

**Flag instead of filter.** Four expressions mark duplicates without
removing them:

```{python}
sightings_df.with_columns(
    is_duplicated=pl.col("tailnum").is_duplicated(),          # every copy of a repeated key
    is_first_distinct=pl.col("tailnum").is_first_distinct(),  # !duplicated(tailnum)
    is_last_distinct=pl.col("tailnum").is_last_distinct(),    # !duplicated(tailnum, fromLast = TRUE)
    is_unique=pl.col("tailnum").is_unique(),                  # keys seen exactly once
)
```

For a key of several columns, wrap them in a struct:
`pl.struct("origin", "dest").is_first_distinct()`. `df.is_duplicated()` flags
whole-row duplicates.

**Counting** (≈ `n_distinct()`): `flights_df.n_unique(subset=["origin", "dest"])`
returns a Python `int` (224 routes); the expression `pl.col("dest").n_unique()`
works in any context; `approx_n_unique()` estimates with HyperLogLog++ when an
exact count is too expensive.

### Rows by position {#sec-verb-slice}

Positions are 0-based, and a negative position counts from the end. That is
Python's convention, not R's: in R a negative index **drops** rows. In
`slice(offset, length)`, a negative offset starts from the end, a negative
length stops that many rows before the end, and no length runs to the end:

```{python}
positions_df = pl.DataFrame({"i": range(10)})
{
    "slice(2, 3)": positions_df.slice(2, 3)["i"].to_list(),      # slice(3:5)
    "slice(-3)": positions_df.slice(-3)["i"].to_list(),          # slice_tail(n = 3)
    "slice(2, -3)": positions_df.slice(2, -3)["i"].to_list(),
    "slice(8, 5)": positions_df.slice(8, 5)["i"].to_list(),      # past the end: clipped
    "head(-3)": positions_df.head(-3)["i"].to_list(),            # slice_head(n = -3)
    "tail(-3)": positions_df.tail(-3)["i"].to_list(),            # slice_tail(n = -3)
    "gather([0, 3, -1])": positions_df.gather([0, 3, -1])["i"].to_list(),  # slice(c(1, 4, n()))
    "gather_every(3)": positions_df.gather_every(3)["i"].to_list(),        # every 3rd row
}
```

`slice()` clips silently, but `gather()` (≈ `slice()` with a vector of
positions) is strict. dplyr silently ignores positions past the end;
`gather()` raises, and `null_on_oob=True` returns a row of nulls instead:

```{python}
#| error: true
positions_df.gather([1, 10])
```

Square brackets do the same jobs: `df[2:5]` is `slice(2, 3)`, `df[[0, 3]]` is
`gather([0, 3])`. The methods chain, and they also work on a `LazyFrame`.

### Rows by value: `top_k()` and `bottom_k()` {#sec-verb-topk}

`top_k(k, by=)` returns the *k* rows with the largest `by` values;
`bottom_k()` the smallest. Several keys are compared like a multi-key sort,
and `reverse=` (one bool, or one per key) flips a key's direction. The
longest flights, ties broken by the largest departure delay:

```{python}
flights_df.top_k(3, by=["distance", "dep_delay"]).select(
    "origin", "dest", "distance", "dep_delay"
)
```

(The most delayed flight of 2013 was the 1,301-minute departure to Honolulu.)
Unlike `sort()`, both verbs rank nulls below every value, so `top_k(3)` and
`sort(descending=True).head(3)` disagree on a column with nulls. Two more
differences from `slice_max()`: exactly *k* rows come back, and the docstring
promises no output order (@sec-verb-ties).

### Random rows: `sample()` {#sec-verb-sample}

`sample()` takes `n` or `fraction` (which rounds down: 0.02 × 344 rows gives
6), `with_replacement=False`, `seed=` (without one, every render draws a
different sample) and `shuffle=`. The last one is the surprise. Its default,
`None`, promises no order, and in practice a sample of every row comes back in
input order. `slice_sample(prop = 1)` shuffles; here you need `shuffle=True`:

```{python}
penguins_df_indexed = penguins_df.with_row_index("row")
{
    "fraction=1": penguins_df_indexed.sample(fraction=1, seed=42)["row"].head(5).to_list(),
    "fraction=1, shuffle=True": penguins_df_indexed.sample(
        fraction=1, shuffle=True, seed=42
    )["row"].head(5).to_list(),
}
```

dplyr's `slice_sample(n = 400)` on 344 rows silently returns 344. Polars
raises unless `with_replacement=True`:

```{python}
#| error: true
penguins_df.sample(400, seed=1)
```

`sample()` is eager-only: `LazyFrame` has no `sample()` method.

### Per-group slices {#sec-verb-groups}

`group_by(g, maintain_order=True).head(n)` and `.tail(n)` are
`slice_head()` / `slice_tail()` with `by =`. Every other per-group slice is a
window predicate in `filter()`, which keeps rows in input order. This is
`slice_max(body_mass_g, n = 2, by = species, with_ties = FALSE)`:

```{python}
penguins_df.filter(
    pl.col("body_mass_g").rank("ordinal", descending=True).over("species") <= 2
).select("species", "island", "body_mass_g")
```

`"ordinal"` breaks ties by position; `"min"` keeps them. A random 2 per group
shuffles a row counter: `pl.int_range(pl.len()).shuffle(seed=1).over("species") < 2`.
More in [Window Functions](window.qmd) and
[Grouping & Aggregation](group-agg.qmd).

### Select, drop, rename {#sec-verb-select}

The cheatsheet maps most of tidyselect
([Select Columns](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-select)). The
column range `year:day` has no verb; on a `DataFrame` a label slice with
square brackets does it, inclusive at both ends:

```{python}
year_to_day = flights_df[:, "year":"day"].columns
year_to_day, flights_df.drop(year_to_day).columns[:3]   # year:day and !year:day
```

On a `LazyFrame`, select by position instead: `cs.by_index(range(0, 3))`.

**`drop()` is strict.** A name that doesn't exist raises, which catches
typos. `strict=False` ignores missing names (≈ `select(-any_of(...))`), and a
selector that matches nothing never raises:

```{python}
#| error: true
flights_df.drop("tail_num")
```

**`rename()` takes `{old: new}`**, the reverse of dplyr's `new = old`, or a
function `str → str` applied to every name. Renamed columns keep their
position, and all renames happen at once, so a swap works:

```{python}
flights_df.select("origin", "dest").head(2).rename({"origin": "dest", "dest": "origin"})
```

An old name that doesn't exist raises unless `strict=False`. A new name that
already exists (and isn't being renamed away) raises a `DuplicateError`. To
rename only some columns with a function (≈ `rename_with(.cols = )`), see
[Selectors](../core/selectors.qmd#sec-sel-recipes).

### Reorder columns {#sec-verb-relocate}

There is no `relocate()`. Moving columns to the front or back is a `select()`
of the moved columns plus everything else. With selectors, "everything else"
is the complement `~` ([Set algebra](../core/selectors.qmd#sec-sel-algebra)):

```{python}
flights_df.select(cs.starts_with("arr"), ~cs.starts_with("arr")).columns[:4]
```

To **create** a column at the front (≈ `mutate(.before = 1)`), pass the new
expression before `pl.all()`. There is no name clash, because the name is new:

```{python}
flights_df.select(
    (pl.col("dep_delay") - pl.col("arr_delay")).alias("gain"), pl.all()
).columns[:4]
```

`.before =` / `.after =` another column needs the name list built in Python
(@sec-verb-recipes).

### Add, replace and index columns {#sec-verb-mutate}

`with_columns()` places each output by name. An existing name is replaced
**in its position**; a new name is appended at the end, in argument order
(keyword arguments come last, see
[Naming](../core/expressions.qmd#sec-expr-naming)):

```{python}
flights_df.select("year", "month", "day", "air_time").head(2).with_columns(
    hours=pl.col("air_time") / 60,          # new name → appended
    month=pl.col("month").cast(pl.Int8),    # existing name → replaced in place
)
```

dplyr's `.keep =` argument has no Polars equivalent, but an expression knows
its inputs (`meta.root_names()`), which is enough to rebuild
`mutate(gain = dep_delay - arr_delay, .keep = "used")`:

```{python}
gain = pl.col("dep_delay") - pl.col("arr_delay")
flights_df.select(*gain.meta.root_names(), gain=gain).head(3)
```

`.keep = "none"` is plain `select()`; `.keep = "unused"` is
`with_columns(gain=gain).drop(gain.meta.root_names())`. And
`with_columns_seq()` is not dplyr's sequential `mutate()`: it runs expressions
one after another instead of in parallel, but a later one still can't see an
earlier one's output.

`with_row_index()` (≈ `rowid_to_column()`) adds the index as the **first**
column, named `index` by default, with dtype `UInt32` (unsigned, see
[Counts are unsigned](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-unsigned)). `offset=`
sets the starting number and must not be negative:

```{python}
penguins_df.with_row_index("id", offset=1).select("id", "species").head(2)
```

## Where it bites {#sec-verb-gotchas}

| tidyverse behaviour | Polars behaviour |
|---|---|
| `arrange()` puts `NA` last | `sort()` puts nulls first, even with `descending=True`; pass `nulls_last=True` |
| `arrange()` keeps tied rows in input order | multi-key `sort()` does not; pass `maintain_order=True` |
| `slice_max()` keeps ties | `top_k()` returns *k* arbitrary rows among ties |
| `distinct()` keeps the first copy, in input order | `unique()` keeps any copy, in an order that changes every call |
| `distinct(x)` drops the other columns | `unique(subset="x")` keeps them |
| `slice(-1)` drops the first row | `slice(-1)` is the last row |
| `slice()` ignores positions past the end | `gather()` raises; `null_on_oob=True` gives a null row |
| `slice_sample(n = 400)` on 344 rows returns 344 | `sample(400)` raises; pass `with_replacement=True` |
| `slice_sample(prop = 1)` shuffles | `sample(fraction=1)` keeps input order unless `shuffle=True` |
| `filter(month = 1)` is an error | `filter(month=1)` means `pl.col("month") == 1` |
| `select(x, everything())` moves `x` first | duplicate output names raise |
| `slice_head(n = 1, by = g)` keeps column order | `group_by("g").head(1)` moves `g` to the front |
| `names(df) <- ...` modifies a copy | `df.columns = ...` and `insert_column()` modify in place |

: The differences at a glance {.striped}

### Nulls sort first, even descending {#sec-verb-nulls-first}

R4DS's `arrange(desc(dep_delay))` shows the most delayed flights. The same
call in Polars shows cancelled ones:

```{python}
flights_df.sort("dep_delay", descending=True).select(
    "month", "day", "carrier", "flight", "dep_delay"
).head(3)
```

With `nulls_last=True`, the first row is the 1,301-minute Honolulu flight from
@sec-verb-topk. **Rule:** pass `nulls_last=True` to every `sort()` that feeds
`head()`, a "first per group", or a report.

### Ties: unstable sorts, arbitrary `top_k()` {#sec-verb-ties}

Number the rows, sort by day, and see where the file's first rows end up:

```{python}
flights_df_indexed = flights_df.with_row_index("row")
by_day_default = flights_df_indexed.sort("month", "day")
by_day_stable = flights_df_indexed.sort("month", "day", maintain_order=True)
{
    "default: first rows": by_day_default["row"].head(5).to_list(),
    "maintain_order: first rows": by_day_stable["row"].head(5).to_list(),
    "rows in a different position": (by_day_default["row"] != by_day_stable["row"]).sum(),
}
```

Every row is in the right day either way, but the default sort reorders rows
within a day: two thirds of all rows land somewhere other than where a stable
sort puts them. The reordering was the same in every run here, and single-key
sorts happened to be stable, but only `maintain_order=True` guarantees either.
It matters as soon as the next step takes "the first row" of each day.

`top_k()` has the same blind spot. 342 flights tie for the longest distance
(JFK → HNL); `slice_max(distance, n = 3)` returns all of them. `top_k()`
returns 3, and not the first 3 in the file:

```{python}
flights_df_indexed.top_k(3, by="distance").select("row", "origin", "dest", "distance")
```

Keep the ties with a rank filter, or make the choice deterministic with a
tie-breaker key (`reverse=` per key: largest distance, then smallest row
number):

```{python}
{
    "ties kept (slice_max)": flights_df.filter(
        pl.col("distance").rank("min", descending=True) <= 3
    ).height,
    "first 3 in file order": flights_df_indexed.top_k(
        3, by=["distance", "row"], reverse=[False, True]
    )["row"].to_list(),
}
```

### `unique()` defaults: any copy, any order {#sec-verb-unique-defaults}

Without `maintain_order=True`, the row order of `unique()` is not just
arbitrary, it changes from call to call:

```{python}
carrier_orders = {tuple(flights_df.unique(subset="carrier")["carrier"]) for _ in range(20)}
len(carrier_orders)   # distinct orderings in 20 identical calls
```

That breaks frozen renders, tests and diffs. The default `keep="any"` is the
same kind of licence: in every probe on 2.0 it returned the first copy, but
the docstring guarantees nothing. When the surviving row matters, spell out
both: `unique(subset=..., keep="first", maintain_order=True)`. Per the
docstring, `maintain_order=True` also keeps that step off the streaming
engine.

### Selections don't deduplicate {#sec-verb-select-dupes}

tidyselect combines selections as a **set**: `select(time_hour, everything())`
names `time_hour` twice and keeps it once, which is the classic way to move a
column to the front. A Polars `select()` is a **list** of expressions, and two
outputs with the same name are an error:

```{python}
#| error: true
flights_df.select("time_hour", pl.all())
```

Exclude it from the rest instead: `select("time_hour", pl.exclude("time_hour"))`.
Selector algebra does deduplicate, but a selector returns columns in **schema
order**, so `select(cs.by_name("time_hour") | cs.all())` leaves `time_hour`
last, where it was.

### Some column verbs work in place {#sec-verb-in-place}

Almost every Polars method returns a new frame. Assigning to `df.columns` and
calling `insert_column()` modify the frame itself instead, so every Python name
bound to that frame sees the change:

```{python}
dates_df = flights_df.select("year", "month", "day").head(2)
same_df = dates_df                        # a second name, not a copy
dates_df.columns = ["yr", "mo", "dy"]     # in place
returned_df = dates_df.insert_column(0, pl.Series("id", [1, 2]))  # in place, too
same_df.columns, returned_df is dates_df
```

R's `names(df) <- ...` is copy-on-modify: another variable bound to the old
frame keeps the old names. `replace_column()` and `drop_in_place()` also work
in place. `rename()`, `with_columns()` and `select()` never do.

## Recipes {#sec-verb-recipes}

**Rows with the max per group, ties kept** (R4DS:
`group_by(dest) |> slice_max(arr_delay, n = 1)`). Compare each row with its
group's max:

```{python}
worst_arrival_df = flights_df.filter(
    pl.col("arr_delay") == pl.col("arr_delay").max().over("dest")
)
worst_arrival_df.height, worst_arrival_df["dest"].n_unique()
```

R4DS gets 108 rows for 105 destinations. The extra one is the single flight to
LGA, whose `arr_delay` is `NA`: with `na_rm = FALSE`, `slice_max()` returns
`NA` rows when a group has nothing else. In Polars that group's max is null,
the comparison is null, and `filter()` drops the row.

**First and last flight of each day.** `datasets.flights()` is not in date
order (the months run 1, 10, 11, 12, 2, …), so "first" needs an explicit sort.
Drop cancelled flights, sort with `maintain_order=True` so equal departure
times keep file order, then keep the first copy per day:

```{python}
flights_df_departed = flights_df.drop_nulls("dep_time").sort(
    "month", "day", "dep_time", maintain_order=True
)
flights_df_departed.unique(
    subset=["month", "day"], keep="first", maintain_order=True
).select("month", "day", "dep_time", "carrier", "flight", "dest").head(3)
```

`keep="last"` gives the last flight of each day.
`group_by("month", "day", maintain_order=True).head(1)` returns the same rows,
but moves `month` and `day` in front of `year`.

**Deduplicate, keeping the latest record**: the last flight of each plane.
Sort by time, then keep the last copy per key. Drop null keys first, because
all nulls count as one key:

```{python}
flights_df.drop_nulls("tailnum").sort("time_hour", maintain_order=True).unique(
    subset="tailnum", keep="last", maintain_order=True
).select("tailnum", "time_hour", "origin", "dest").head(3)
```

`maintain_order=True` orders the result by each plane's last flight, so the
top rows are planes last seen leaving New York in the first days of January.

**Move columns before or after another** (≈ `relocate(.before =, .after =)`).
Build the name list in Python; `cs.expand_selector()` turns a selector into
names, so tidyselect-style arguments work too:

```{python}
def relocate(df, columns, *, before=None, after=None):
    """Move `columns` (names or a selector) before/after an anchor column."""
    if cs.is_selector(columns):
        columns = cs.expand_selector(df, columns)
    columns = [columns] if isinstance(columns, str) else list(columns)
    rest = [c for c in df.columns if c not in columns]
    if before is not None:
        at = rest.index(before)
    elif after is not None:
        at = rest.index(after) + 1
    else:
        at = 0
    return df.select(rest[:at] + columns + rest[at:])

relocate(flights_df, cs.starts_with("arr"), before="dep_time").columns[:7]
```
